name: Free State of Prussia
info: The largest state of the Weimar Republic, a parliamentary democracy governed mostly by Social Democrats, deposed by the Prussian coup of 1932, absorbed by the Nazi regime and abolished by the Allies in 1947.

facts.founder: The revolutionary government of the MSPD and USPD under Paul Hirsch, November 1918
facts.successor: Divided among Poland, the Soviet Union and the post-war German states

t: Prussia held roughly three fifths of Germany's territory and population and became a parliamentary democracy under its constitution of 30 November 1920.
Under Minister President Otto Braun and Interior Minister Carl Severing it was considered a bulwark of democracy within the Weimar Republic.
Franz von Papen's Prussian coup d'état of July 1932 removed its government; under Hermann Göring it served the Nazi regime until the Allied Control Council abolished it on 25 February 1947.
dyk: The Gestapo grew out of the Prussian political police, which came under Hermann Göring after Hitler named him Reich commissioner of the Interior for Prussia in 1933.
ev: On 12 November representatives of the Berlin workers' and soldiers' councils declare the previous Prussian government deposed
The Prussian State Assembly is elected on 26 January and the Weimar Coalition forms a government in March
The Kapp Putsch collapses after six days; Otto Braun becomes minister president and the constitution is adopted on 30 November
French and Belgian troops occupy the Ruhr, and a Rhenish Republic survives less than a month
Blood May costs 33 lives in Berlin, and the Prussian Concordat with the Vatican is signed on 14 June
After the Altona Bloody Sunday, Hindenburg appoints Papen Reich commissioner for Prussia on 20 July
Göring becomes Prussian minister president, and the Landtag meets for the last time on 18 May
Control Council Law No. 46 of 25 February decrees the dissolution of Prussia

sections.foundation:
The German revolution, begun by the sailors' mutiny at Kiel, reached Berlin on 9 November 1918, when Max von Baden announced the abdication of Wilhelm II as Emperor and King of Prussia. Friedrich Ebert charged Paul Hirsch of the MSPD with keeping order in Prussia, and on 12 November councils' representatives declared the old government deposed, promising to make Prussia a fully democratic part of the unified republic. A revolutionary cabinet of the MSPD and USPD, chaired jointly by Hirsch and Heinrich Ströbel, confiscated the royal property and abolished the House of Lords on 15 November.

Prussia's survival was not assured: the Centre Party's council in the Rhine Province called for a Rhineland-Westphalian republic, 600,000 signed for autonomy in Hanover, and a revolt in Posen aimed at restoring Poland. Hugo Preuss envisaged breaking Prussia up. The State Assembly, elected on 26 January 1919 by universal suffrage that replaced the three-class franchise, resolved against a breakup, and a Weimar Coalition of the MSPD, Centre and DDP governed from March 1919.
sections.socioeconomy:
Prussia had roughly three fifths of Germany's territory and population; 61% of Germany's people lived there in 1925. Its density, 130.7 inhabitants per square kilometre, hid large contrasts: 60.9 in East Prussia against 295.6 in the Rhine Province. In 1925 industry and the skilled trades employed 41.3% of workers, agriculture 22% and trade and transport 17.5%, but in East Prussia agriculture employed 45.4%, and the agrarian east remained distinct from the industrial west.

Of those employed in 1925, 46.8% were blue-collar workers, 17.1% salaried employees and civil servants and 16.2% self-employed. In 1928 average income in Berlin-Brandenburg was 1,566 Reichsmarks, more than 30% above the national average, while East Prussia's was 814. Greater Berlin was formed in 1920 by incorporating 8 cities and 59 rural communities. The Braun government abolished the 12,000 manorial districts, home to 1.5 million people, in 1927, though in 1928 83% of an average East Prussian farm worker's income still came as wages in kind. The pupil-teacher ratio fell from 55 in 1911 to 38 in 1928.
sections.military:
Prussia lost its army with the transfer of military responsibilities to the national government, and there was no Prussian Minister of War after 1919. Its force was the police, the strongest in Germany and the government's chief instrument for keeping constitutional order. Early violence was heavy: fighting with the People's Navy Division in December 1918 was followed by the Spartacist uprising of 5–12 January 1919, with an estimated 150 to 200 dead, strikes of 350,000 Ruhr miners and the first Silesian uprising of August 1919, put down by military means.

After the Kapp Putsch of March 1920, backed chiefly by the large landowners of East Elbia, Severing and the police chief Wilhelm Abegg made the force loyal to the Republic; by 1928 fifteen of thirty police chiefs were Social Democrats, though the rank and file remained largely conservative. Prussia banned the Nazi Party in 1922, the Red Front Fighters after Blood May in 1929 and the SA in 1931. After 1933 the police under Göring became an important element in enforcing Nazi rule.
sections.governance:
The constitution adopted on 30 November 1920, by 280 votes to 60, gave Prussia no state president. The Landtag, elected for four years, chose the minister president, who had policy-making authority and appointed the other ministers. A State Council elected by the provincial parliaments, chaired until 1933 by Konrad Adenauer, could initiate laws and object to them. There were twelve provinces plus Berlin, each with a governor (Oberpräsident) and a parliament, and 361 rural and 116 urban districts.

With brief interruptions the SPD held the premiership: Hirsch, Adam Stegerwald in 1921, a grand coalition under Otto Braun from November 1921 to 1925, Wilhelm Marx briefly, and Braun again from 3 April 1925. The "Braun-Severing system" purged the administration of republic-hostile officials: about a hundred senior civil servants were retired, and by 1929 291 of 540 political officials belonged to the coalition parties. The judiciary resisted reform; one estimate of 1932 held that only about 5% of judges were republican-minded.
sections.impact:
Prussia was more politically stable than the Republic itself. Gustav Stresemann called the Prussia of 1923 the "bulwark of German republicans", and its grand coalition helped the Republic survive that crisis year. The SPD's readiness to govern in Prussia, which it lacked nationally in 1920, 1923 and 1930, was one reason; Otto Braun claimed that Prussia had never been governed in a more Prussian manner than during his term. Joseph Goebbels wrote in 1930 that whoever had Prussia also had the Reich.

The Free State also reshaped religion and education. The Prussian Concordat with the Vatican, signed on 14 June 1929 by Eugenio Pacelli, ended the last church laws of the Kulturkampf and re-established the bishoprics of Aachen and Berlin, while a treaty with the Protestant churches followed in 1931. Its territory, however, bore most of Germany's losses under the Treaty of Versailles: Eupen-Malmedy, the Hultschiner Ländchen, Danzig, the Memel Territory and much of Posen and West Prussia, leaving East Prussia cut off by the Polish Corridor.
sections.decline:
In the Landtag election of 1932 the NSDAP rose from 1.8% to 36.7% and, with the KPD, held a negative majority; Braun's caretaker government stayed in office. After 18 people died in the Altona Bloody Sunday on 17 July, Hindenburg used Article 48 to dismiss the Prussian ministers and appoint Franz von Papen Reich commissioner. On 25 October 1932 the Reich Constitutional Court in Leipzig found the removal illegal, but Prussia was left with two governments, one without power.

After Hitler became chancellor, Göring took over the Prussian Interior, the Landtag was dissolved and, after the March 1933 election, confirmed the dismissal of the Braun government. The coordination laws of 31 March and 7 April subordinated Prussia to the Reich, Göring became minister president on 11 April, and the Landtag met for the last time on 18 May 1933, the SPD alone refusing the enabling act. The laws of 1934 and 1935 dissolved the states in fact. In 1945 the lands east of the Oder–Neisse line went to Poland and the Soviet Union and an estimated twelve million Germans fled or were expelled; Control Council Law No. 46 of 25 February 1947 dissolved Prussia, the Allies citing its history of militarism.

summary: The Free State of Prussia was the dominant state of Weimar Germany, a democracy led mostly by the SPD's Otto Braun and Carl Severing that reformed its civil service and police and was called a bulwark of the Republic. The Prussian coup of 1932 and the Nazi seizure of power hollowed it out, and the Allies abolished it in 1947.
references: Orlow, Dietrich, Weimar Prussia, 1925–1933: The Illusion of Strength (University of Pittsburgh Press, 1991)
Ziblatt, Daniel, Conservative Parties and the Birth of Democracy (Cambridge University Press, 2017)

pointDescs.1918: The revolution deposes the royal government and a cabinet of the MSPD and USPD takes over Prussia.
pointDescs.1919: The State Assembly is elected and the Weimar Coalition forms a government.
pointDescs.1920: The Kapp Putsch fails, Braun and Severing take office and the constitution is adopted.
pointDescs.1921: The first regular Landtag is elected and a grand coalition under Braun is formed.
pointDescs.1923: The Ruhr occupation and hyperinflation strike Prussia's western provinces; it holds as the bulwark of the republicans.
pointDescs.1925: Braun is elected minister president again on 3 April and heads a remarkably stable cabinet.
pointDescs.1928: The coalition keeps its majority with 228 of 450 seats.
pointDescs.1930: The Nazis rise in the Reichstag; Prussia keeps its bans on Nazi uniforms and Severing returns to the Interior.
pointDescs.1932: The NSDAP becomes the strongest party, and the Prussian coup d'état removes the government.
pointDescs.1933: Prussia is subordinated to the Reich, Göring becomes minister president and the Landtag meets for the last time.
pointDescs.1935: The Reich Governors Law completes the dissolution of the states in fact if not in law.
pointDescs.1945: Germany is occupied and the lands east of the Oder–Neisse line are ceded to Poland and the Soviet Union.
pointDescs.1947: Control Council Law No. 46 abolishes Prussia on 25 February.

notes: Capital Berlin: the article says Prussia 'was home to the federal capital Berlin' and Berlin was one of its provinces; it does not name a Prussian capital as such. The 1934 'Law on the Reconstruction of the Reich' is dated 30 January 1934 in the article. 'Agricultural' tag is weak; Prussia's economy was industrial in the west - editor may prefer 'Commercial'.
